lead: Shear in a reinforced concrete beam shows itself as diagonal tension in the web. Bending and shear stress combine into a principal tension inclined to the beam axis, and because concrete is weak in tension, inclined cracks open long before the steel yields. After cracking, the beam carries shear through the uncracked concrete above the crack, friction across the crack, dowel action of the main bars and the stirrups. Every shear rule in IS 456 comes from this picture.
prereq: You need: the singly reinforced section, effective depth d and the limit state of collapse (limit state design of beams). The stirrup design itself is in Design of shear reinforcement.

sections.h3: Diagonal tension in an uncracked beam

blocks.text: Take a point inside a beam. Bending gives a horizontal normal stress σ there (compression above the neutral axis, tension below it). The shear force V gives a shear stress τ, equal on the horizontal and the vertical plane through the point. The two combine into a principal tensile stress σ<sub>1</sub> acting on an inclined plane.

blocks.where: σ<sub>1</sub> is the principal tensile stress; σ is the bending stress, positive in tension (N/mm²); τ = V Q/(I b) is the shear stress, with Q the first moment of the area beyond the point about the neutral axis (mm³), I the second moment of area (mm⁴) and b the width (mm); θ is the angle of σ<sub>1</sub> to the beam axis.

blocks.text: At the soffit τ = 0, so σ<sub>1</sub> is horizontal and the crack is vertical. At the neutral axis σ = 0, so σ<sub>1</sub> = τ at θ = 45°. A crack that starts vertical at the soffit therefore bends over towards the load as it climbs: a flexure-shear crack, the usual shear crack. In a thin web near a support an inclined web-shear crack can open first at the neutral axis. Concrete cracks when σ<sub>1</sub> reaches its tensile strength, only about 2 to 3 N/mm² for M25.

sections.h3: How a cracked beam carries shear

blocks.text: Cut the beam along an inclined crack and look at the piece between the crack and the support. The shear on that piece is held by four forces.

blocks.where: V<sub>cz</sub> is the shear in the uncracked compression zone; V<sub>a</sub> is the vertical part of aggregate interlock, friction between the rough crack faces; V<sub>d</sub> is the dowel force in the main bars crossing the crack; V<sub>s</sub> is the sum of the stirrup forces crossing the crack.

blocks.text: Aggregate interlock works only while the crack is narrow, and dowel action is limited by the thin cover under the bars. Stirrups do almost nothing before cracking; after it they are the part that can be designed, and by holding the crack narrow they keep V<sub>a</sub> and V<sub>d</sub> working too.

The truss analogy puts these together: the compression zone is the top chord, the tension steel the bottom chord, the concrete between cracks forms 45° struts and the stirrups are the vertical ties. A stirrup inclined at 45° against the crack crosses it at 90° and works better than a vertical one, but vertical stirrups are easier to fix and also hold the main bars.
Without enough shear steel, the failure mode depends mainly on a/d, where a is the shear span (point load to support).

items: a/d below about 1 (deep beams): arch action; the strut crushes or splits, or the tie bars lose anchorage.
a/d about 1 to 2.5: shear-compression; the concrete above the inclined crack crushes.
a/d about 2.5 to 6: diagonal tension; the crack runs through suddenly and the beam splits. The most brittle mode.
Thin webs under heavy shear: web crushing of the struts, which stirrups cannot prevent.

sections.h3: From behaviour to the code check

blocks.where: τ<sub>v</sub> is the nominal shear stress (N/mm²); V<sub>u</sub> is the factored shear force at the section (N); b is the width of the beam, or the web width b<sub>w</sub> of a flanged beam (mm); d is the effective depth (mm).

blocks.text: τ<sub>c</sub> is the design shear strength of concrete (IS 456 Table 19). It rises with the grade and with p<sub>t</sub> = 100 A<sub>st</sub>/(b d), where A<sub>st</sub> is the tension steel (mm²) continuing at least d beyond the section. τ<sub>c,max</sub> (Table 20) caps τ<sub>v</sub> even with shear steel, to stop web crushing: 2.8 N/mm² for M20, 3.1 for M25, 3.5 for M30.

So there are three cases: τ<sub>v</sub> ≤ τ<sub>c</sub> needs only minimum stirrups; τ<sub>c</sub> < τ<sub>v</sub> ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub> needs stirrups designed for V<sub>us</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub> b d; τ<sub>v</sub> > τ<sub>c,max</sub> needs a bigger section or a higher grade.

Where the support reaction compresses the beam end, load within d of the support face goes straight into the support, so IS 456 takes the section at d from the face as critical and designs the zone nearer the support for that shear.

examples.question: An uncracked M25 beam 300 mm × 600 mm carries M = 60 kN·m and V = 120 kN at a section. Treating it as a plain concrete section, find σ, τ, σ<sub>1</sub> and its direction 150 mm below the neutral axis, and σ<sub>1</sub> at the neutral axis. Compare with the flexural strength 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub>.
steps: I = b D³/12 = 300 × 600³/12 = 5.4 × 10⁹ mm⁴, with the neutral axis at mid-depth.
Bending stress at y = 150 mm (tension side): σ = M y/I = 60 × 10⁶ × 150/(5.4 × 10⁹) = 1.67 N/mm².
Area below the point: 300 × 150 = 45,000 mm² with centroid 225 mm from the axis, so Q = 1.0125 × 10⁷ mm³ and τ = V Q/(I b) = 120 × 10³ × 1.0125 × 10⁷/(5.4 × 10⁹ × 300) = 0.75 N/mm².
σ<sub>1</sub> = 0.833 + √(0.833² + 0.75²) = 0.833 + 1.121 = 1.95 N/mm²; tan 2θ = 1.5/1.667 = 0.90, so θ = 21.0°. The crack would form at right angles to σ<sub>1</sub>, at 69° to the axis.
At the neutral axis: σ<sub>1</sub> = τ<sub>max</sub> = 1.5 V/(b D) = 1.5 × 120,000/180,000 = 1.00 N/mm² at 45°.
Flexural strength of M25: 0.7 √25 = 3.5 N/mm². Both values are below it, so the beam is still uncracked.
examples.answer: σ = 1.67 N/mm² (tension), τ = 0.75 N/mm², σ<sub>1</sub> = 1.95 N/mm² at 21° to the axis (a crack would form at 69°); at the neutral axis σ<sub>1</sub> = 1.00 N/mm² at 45°. Both are below 3.5 N/mm², so no crack yet.
examples.check:
import math
I=300*600**3/12
s=60e6*150/I
Q=300*150*225
t=120e3*Q/(I*300)
s1=s/2+math.sqrt((s/2)**2+t*t)
th=math.degrees(math.atan(2*t/s))/2
print(round(s,2),round(t,2),round(s1,2),round(th,1),round(1.5*120e3/(300*600),2))

examples.question: The same beam, now cracked, has effective depth d = 550 mm and three 25 mm bars in tension continuing past the section. The factored shear at the critical section is V<sub>u</sub> = 180 kN; concrete is M25. Find τ<sub>v</sub>, p<sub>t</sub>, τ<sub>c</sub> (IS 456 Table 19) and τ<sub>c,max</sub>, decide which case applies, and find the shear the stirrups must carry.
steps: Table 19, M25: τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57 at p<sub>t</sub> = 0.75 and 0.64 at 1.00, so τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57 + (0.89 − 0.75)/0.25 × 0.07 = 0.61 N/mm². Table 20: τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm².
τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.61 < τ<sub>v</sub> = 1.09 < τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm²: the section is adequate, but shear reinforcement must be designed.
Concrete share: τ<sub>c</sub> b d = 0.61 × 165,000 = 100.65 kN. Stirrup share: V<sub>us</sub> = 180 − 100.65 = 79.35 kN.
examples.answer: τ<sub>v</sub> = 1.09 N/mm², p<sub>t</sub> = 0.89 %, τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.61 N/mm², τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm²; the middle case applies, and the stirrups must carry V<sub>us</sub> = 79.35 kN (designed in the next chapter).

traps: Writing that the crack is along the principal tension. It opens at right angles to σ<sub>1</sub>: 45° at the neutral axis, but 69° at the point of worked example 1.
Treating τ<sub>c</sub> as fixed for a grade. It also depends on p<sub>t</sub>, counting only bars that continue at least d past the section.
Thinking more stirrups cure web crushing. Above τ<sub>c,max</sub> only a bigger section or a higher grade helps.
Using D instead of d in τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(b d), or leaving V<sub>u</sub> in kN instead of N.

quiz.q: What is diagonal tension in a reinforced concrete beam?
quiz.a: The principal tensile stress produced by bending and shear together. It acts on inclined planes, at 45° at the neutral axis, and causes inclined cracks.

quiz.q: Why is the critical section for shear taken at d from the face of a support?
quiz.a: When the reaction compresses the beam end, load placed within d of the face travels straight into the support by arch action, and a full inclined crack cannot form there. IS 456 lets that zone be designed for the shear at d.

quiz.q: A beam has b = 250 mm, d = 450 mm, V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN and p<sub>t</sub> = 0.50 % in M20 concrete. Find τ<sub>v</sub>, read τ<sub>c</sub> and say what is required.
quiz.a: τ<sub>v</sub> = 120 × 10³/(250 × 450) = 1.07 N/mm². Table 19, M20, p<sub>t</sub> = 0.50: τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.48 N/mm². τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 2.8 N/mm². Since 0.48 < 1.07 < 2.8, design stirrups for V<sub>us</sub> = 120 − 0.48 × 250 × 450/1000 = 120 − 54 = 66 kN.

quiz.q: A point load is 1.2 m from the support of a beam with d = 400 mm. Which shear failure mode do you expect if the beam has no stirrups?
quiz.a: a/d = 1200/400 = 3.0, which lies between 2.5 and 6, so diagonal tension failure: a sudden inclined crack that splits the beam.

quiz.q: Why does aggregate interlock depend on the stirrups even though stirrups and aggregate interlock are different mechanisms?
quiz.a: Aggregate interlock works only while the crack faces stay close together. Stirrups crossing the crack hold it narrow, so the faces keep bearing on each other. Without stirrups the crack widens and V<sub>a</sub> and V<sub>d</sub> fall quickly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Deep beams, pile caps and corbels, where the shear span is short, are designed by strut-and-tie models, a direct extension of the truss analogy. Newer codes predict the concrete shear strength from crack width with the modified compression field theory. Search for 'strut-and-tie model', 'modified compression field theory' and 'size effect in shear'.
